content_list.content_text: "Black film may be to the '90s what the car phone was to the '80s: every studio executive has to have one," wrote The New York Times magazine in the summer of 1991. It is a comment that says a lot about a cultural moment and its transience. The article was titled They've Gotta Have Us, a reference to the film by Spike Lee (b. 1957) released in 1986, She's Gotta Have It (1986).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Do the Right Thing
information.contentText: The film tells the story of racial tension in the borough of Brooklyn (New York), which comes to the surface and culminates in tragedy on a hot summer day. The film was a critical and box office success, receiving numerous accolades and awards, including Oscar nominations for Lee for Best Original Screenplay and for Aiello's performance in the Best Supporting Actor category.

content_list.content_text: The group portrait on the cover brought together an impressive collection of young Black filmmakers, what was labeled “the class of '91.” Lee was at the top, of course. At the time, he was in the midst of a creative burst that would continue at a pace of practically one film a year: Do the Right Thing (1989), Mo' Better Blues (1990), Jungle Fever (1991), Malcolm X (1992), Crooklyn (1994), Clockers (1995).

content_list.title: Boyz n the Hood: An Honest Portrait of a Society
content_list.description:
Thanks to forerunners in the early 1970s such as Melvin Van Peebles (b. 1932) and Gordon Parks (1912-2006), a number of African American filmmakers emerged in commercial cinema. Among them, Robert Townsend and Spike Lee deserve special mention, each producing brilliant comic dramas about the condition of Black people in the United States. But it was the autobiographical debut of John Singleton, Boyz n the Hood, in 1991, that introduced critics to a so-called cinematic voice of Black Americans. For his achievement, Singleton received two Oscar nominations, and his film was a surprise hit that earned Columbia Pictures an impressive profit.

Singleton's drama, which begins in the wake of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, tells the story of three 10-year-old boys: Tre (Desi Arnez Hines II), Doughboy (Baha Jackson) and Ricky (Donovan McCrary). Raised by separated parents, they live in a world torn apart by gang violence, police brutality and economic hardship. When Tre's mother, Reva (Angela Bassett), drops him off at the door of his father, Jason "Furious" Styles (Laurence Fishburne), he gets a drastic lesson in manhood and becomes a teenager determined to get ahead in life.

The film jumps ahead seven years. Tre (played from then on by Cuba Gooding Jr.) is a high school senior who works part-time, wants to attend a historically Black college and is dating a young woman named Brandi (Nia Long). Doughboy (Ice Cube) is a layabout gang member who takes advantage of the patience of his mother, Mrs. Baker (Tyra Ferrell), while his brother Ricky (Morris Chestnut) trains, hoping for a college football scholarship. Even while trying to get out of that neighborhood, Tre remains tied to his friends from the block. When thugs from a rival gang threaten the trio, Ricky ends up dead, murdered by a gang. After that, Tre heeds his father's wise teachings and manages to avoid the mistakes of his tyrannized world. In the end, he escapes the trap of poverty and violence and goes off to college with Brandi.

Preachy, but wisely orchestrated as a moving portrait of intraracial violence in America's inner cities, Boyz n the Hood is a fable with a hard-to-forget moral, aimed at the very youth it depicts on screen. After a troubling dedication reminding viewers how many young Black men are murdered by other young Black men, the film launches into a realistic, profanity-laden and moving coming-of-age story.

Also notable as rapper Ice Cube's screen debut, Singleton's film displays full awareness of Hollywood conventions in its storytelling and shows genuine affection for the influence of hip-hop. Structured in three very distinct acts and with a clear leaning toward broad moralizing, the film has a professional polish. But it is also suffused with hypnotic beats and raps by several successful artists who contributed to the soundtrack, making Boyz n the Hood a career-making success and the origin of a wave of dramas centered on Black neighborhoods that flooded screens in the 1990s.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Garret Chaffin-Quiray, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: There was also Lee's friend Ernest Dickerson (b. 1951), cinematographer of Do the Right Thing, who was now directing his own Harlem tale, Juice (1992). There was Mario Van Peebles (b. 1957), creator of the gangster thriller New Jack City (1991). There were the brothers Warrington Hudlin (b. 1952) and Reginald Hudlin (b. 1961), creators of the hit teen comedy House Party (1990). There were Charles Lane (b. 1953) and 20-year-old Matty Rich (b. 1971), whose debut films won awards at Cannes and Sundance, respectively.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Boyz n the Hood
information.contentText: Singleton initially developed the film as an application requirement for film school in 1986 and sold the screenplay to Columbia Pictures upon graduating in 1990. While writing, he drew on his own life and the lives of people he knew, and he insisted on directing the project. The film is notable for being shot in sequence and features key roles for Ice Cube, Gooding Jr. and Nia Long.

content_list.content_text: And the rising star of the moment was John Singleton (1968-2019), whose autobiographical Los Angeles drama Boyz n the Hood (1991) earned him a three-year deal with the studio and would make him the first African American (and the youngest person) to be nominated for the Best Director Oscar. “The current crop is breaking new ground with its stories and politics,” the article observed. “For the studios, these are tales from a new world, presented with an often harrowing, if sometimes hyperbolic, realism.” The filmmakers themselves seemed sensibly wary of being lumped into a trend. “If one Black filmmaker messes up,” said Lee, “they make the rest of us feel it.”

quote.quote: One of those stories with the quality of a nightmare, in which foolish young people try to hurt themselves until they are trapped in a violent situation that will change their lives forever.
quote.author: Roger Ebert on Juice

content_list.content_text: The caution was justified. Fast-forward 25 years or so and we find ourselves in a situation where, for the second year in a row, no African American actor received an Oscar nomination; where they still complain about the lack of representation in film and television, when they are not taking to the streets to remind the country that their lives matter. Did somebody get it wrong?

information.contentText: There was some controversy over the film and how it portrayed racism and racial stereotypes. According to Rose, "I had to go and have a whole series of meetings with the NAACP because the producers were very worried, and what they said to me when they read the script was 'Why are we even having this meeting? You know, this is just fun.' Their argument was 'Why shouldn't a black actor be a ghost? Why shouldn't a black actor play Freddy Krueger or Hannibal Lecter? If you're saying they can't be, that's really perverse. This is a horror movie.'" At the time of the film's release, Madsen said: "I was, and am now, concerned about how people are going to respond. I don't think Spike Lee is going to like this movie."

content_list.content_text: One thing is certain: looking back, the '90s were a golden age. The number of films directed by and starring Black artists that were successful at the time is astonishing. Hip-hop, and white audiences' interest in it, fueled the movement. Rappers and musicians made a seamless transition to film: Ice Cube (b. 1969), Ice-T (b. 1958), Tupac Shakur (1971-1996), Queen Latifah (b. 1970). It was not just youth “hood dramas,” however; there was quality work across the whole spectrum. Serious thrillers such as Devil in a Blue Dress (1995) and Deep Cover (1992) appeared alongside "art" films from the “LA Rebellion” group. This movement of young film students produced influential works such as To Sleep with Anger (1990), by Charles Burnett (b. 1944), and Daughters of the Dust (1991), by Julie Dash (b. 1962), released in 1991, the first feature film directed by an African American woman to receive theatrical distribution in the United States.

content_list.title: L.A. Rebellion
content_list.description: Between the 1970s and 1980s, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) launched a policy of including young film students from diasporic and immigrant backgrounds in the US. It was in this context that an extraordinary body of films emerged, expressing the vigor, singularity, persistence and resonance of a new Black cinema, acclaimed by international critics and claimed by new generations of filmmakers. Rediscovered and restored this decade, the films by African American filmmakers who came out of these classes, driven by a project of historical autonomy and artistic emancipation, were brought together under the label L.A. Rebellion, which came to designate the work of names who would become celebrated, such as Charles Burnett (winner of an honorary Oscar in 2018) and Julie Dash (the first Black woman to direct a commercially released feature film in the US), as well as others who are less well known (but equally remarkable), such as Zeinabu irene Davis, Alile Sharon Larkin, Haile Gerima, Larry Clark and Billy Woodberry.

content_list.content_text: On television, too, African American content seemed to be transforming. Will Smith (b. 1968) figuratively entered Hollywood with The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, while Jamie Foxx (b. 1967) began working on the Wayans brothers' sketch show In Living Color. If you couldn't choose between Friends or Seinfeld, you could find Black-led series such as Moesha, A Different World, Family Matters, Kenan & Kel, Martin, Living Single, Sister, Sister and Malcolm & Eddie.

information.contentText: The film follows Bobby Taylor's attempts to become a successful actor and the mental and external roadblocks he encounters, depicted through a series of interspersed vignettes and fantasies. Produced, directed and co-written by Robert Townsend, the film is semi-autobiographical, reflecting Townsend's experiences as a Black actor who was told he was not "Black enough" for certain roles.

content_list.content_text: For the first time, mainstream film and TV audiences were getting honest, intelligent portrayals of modern African American life and of US history from a Black perspective, the kind of story only Black filmmakers could tell. The revolution was being televised, dramatized, publicized and praised. It is worth remembering that just three years earlier, in 1987, Robert Townsend (b. 1957) had made the cult satire Hollywood Shuffle (1987), which detailed the futile struggle of an aspiring Black actor, and it seems to belong to a completely different era. “The only roles they'll let us play are a slave, a butler or some street thug,” another participant at the audition tells Townsend's character. The white producers say they are looking for an “Eddie Murphy type” and ask him to “be more Black.” In his daydreams, Townsend fantasizes about playing a detective in film noir, a Shakespearean king, a superhero, even a Black Rambo. Instead, he lands the role of a stereotypical street hustler, which only conjures up visions of protesters picketing his house, accusing him of selling out.

But by the mid-'90s, Townsend's wildest dreams had come true. Now you could be a Black Shakespearean, as Denzel Washington (b. 1954) was in Much Ado About Nothing (1993), or a Black superhero, as Wesley Snipes (b. 1962) was in Blade (1998), and not exactly a Rambo, but an action movie hero, as Will Smith (b. 1968) was in Bad Boys (1995).

information.contentText: Cooper's rewrite was adapted from his December 1987 cover story for The Village Voice, titled "Kids Killing Kids: New Jack City Eats Its Young," about the drug war in Detroit. The piece referred to the 20th anniversary of the 1967 Detroit riot and, in its wake, the rise of crack gangs in the late 1980s, such as Young Boys Inc. and the Chambers Brothers.

content_list.content_text: The fruit of that creative flowering of the '90s was a generation of African American artists who gained real Hollywood power: the power to take on leading roles, to win awards and, ultimately, to get films greenlit. Most of them were men, which tells its own story, and most of them still wield that power today: Washington, Smith, Foxx, Samuel L. Jackson. But it was also the time when Angela Bassett (b. 1958) became the first Black woman in more than a decade to receive a Best Actress Oscar nomination, for the Tina Turner biopic What's Love Got to Do with It (1993), and Whitney Houston (1963-2012) powered hits such as The Bodyguard (1992) and (alongside Bassett) Waiting to Exhale (1995).

quote.quote: How do you think the crack rock gets into the country? We don't own any planes. We don't own no ships.
quote.author: Jason "Furious" Styles (Laurence Fishburne) in Boyz n the Hood

content_list.content_text: But did this success come at a cost? The actors were getting the roles, but their films were not necessarily “Black” stories. More often than not, they became token Black faces in regular Hollywood movies: exceptions that proved the rule, you might say. Meanwhile, the filmmakers who had helped put them there seemed to have been left behind. A big part of the problem, says Julie Dash, was that the rise of Black cinema coincided with Hollywood's takeover of independent film as a whole. “It became a commodity that could be co-opted by the industry. We moved forward and, as soon as the curators of culture recognized that we were actively making films our own way, suddenly the thing stopped. The funding dried up for almost everyone.”

information.contentText: The film dramatizes key events in Malcolm's life: his criminal career, his incarceration, his conversion to Islam, his ministry as a member of the Nation of Islam and his later falling-out with the organization, his marriage to Betty X, his pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca and his reassessment of his views on white people, and his assassination on February 21, 1965. Defining incidents, including his father's death, his mother's mental illness, and his experiences with racism, are dramatized in flashbacks.

content_list.content_text: Directors such as Singleton, Dickerson and Van Peebles struggled to regain momentum after becoming Hollywood properties. Lee's career took the shape of an ongoing battle. Clark points out that he had a terrible time making Malcolm X, for example. “He had to fight off competition from other studios to make it. Norman Jewison wanted to make it. His studio, Warner Bros., wouldn't increase the budget, so he had to campaign for people like Prince, Michael Jackson and Oprah Winfrey to fund it.” By the end of the decade, his audience had dwindled, even if the quality of his output had not. Films such as Crooklyn and Bamboozled flopped at the box office, and he ended up making 25th Hour (2002).

content_list.title: The Landmark of a New Wave in Black Cinema
content_list.description:
Living now in a global pop culture so thoroughly sculpted by the language, music, aesthetics and politics of hip-hop, it is sometimes hard to remember that there was a time when the force of that youth movement had not yet been tapped. At the same time, considering the artistic shallowness and materialism that have come to define contemporary hip-hop, it is sometimes equally hard to remember the time when the movement and the music that drove it were radical, subversive and proudly revolutionary. Spike Lee's social protest film brilliantly captures that time when hip-hop and rap were urgent and conscious: perhaps even more impressively, it manages to concentrate the issues of racism, racial pride, class struggle and the joys and frictions of urban life into a snapshot of paradoxically saturated colors. Incendiary and insightful. This is a film born of hip-hop when hip-hop had something to say.

The film opens to the furious music of veteran hip-hop icon Public Enemy. With a cast of vibrant characters whose stories intersect over the course of the day and are used to illuminate larger sociopolitical issues, the film centers on Mookie (Lee), a pizza delivery man who circulates throughout the neighborhood making his deliveries. We meet his demanding, shrill-voiced girlfriend (Rosie Perez), bickering but likable elders (Ruby Dee and Ossie Davis), and neighborhood youths, represented by Radio Raheem (Bill Nunn) and Buggin' Out (Giancarlo Esposito), among others. We also meet the Italian owner of the pizzeria, Sal (Danny Aiello), whose ambivalence about his Black clientele is reflected in the differing attitudes of his racist son Pino (John Turturro) and the more color-blind kid, Vito (Richard Edson). Rounding out the ensemble is a hilarious, profane Greek chorus of elderly and middle-aged Black men whose critical commentary on the day's events offers comic counterpoint.

As the summer day wears on and tempers flare, trivial disagreements take on great significance. Sexual and racial tensions that lie just beneath the surface of everyday encounters explode, and the resulting fierce violence is a clear metaphor for the state of American race relations at the end of the 20th century. Controversial and often misread by its detractors (many of whom said the film was an incitement to riot), Do the Right Thing is an unabashedly angry film. It is also full of images of love and camaraderie among Black people that remain so rare in American cinema that they have become radical. Shot in vivid colors that seem to leap off the screen, full of slightly tilted camera angles that suggest the free style of comic books, and edited to reflect the energetic drive of the most frenetic rap. Do the Right Thing became one of the most influential films in recent film history, not only for its stylistic flourishes but also for giving filmmakers permission to draw on life experiences that until then had been ignored or distorted both in Hollywood and in so-called independent films. It dares you not to take it seriously.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Ernest Hardy, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: But what other options did Lee and company have? “What people don't realize is that he gets tarred and feathered as this angry, political Black man, but he's an artist and he's constantly working,” says Clark. “He works on documentaries, he works on commercials, he never stops. And he has to. He can't, like other directors, just go away for eight years and come back and make something whenever he wants.”
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "Black films matter – how African American cinema fought back against Hollywood," by Steve Rose in The Guardian.

movies.overview: Salvatore "Sal" Fragione is the Italian owner of a pizzeria in Brooklyn. A neighborhood local, Buggin' Out, becomes upset when he sees that the pizzeria's Wall of Fame exhibits only Italian actors. Buggin' Out believes a pizzeria in a black neighborhood should showcase black actors, but Sal disagrees. The wall becomes a symbol of racism and hate to Buggin' Out and to other people in the neighborhood, and tensions rise.
movies.title: Do the Right Thing

movies.overview: Boyz n the Hood is the popular and successful film and social criticism from John Singleton about the conditions in South Central Los Angeles where teenagers are involved in gun fights and drug dealing on a daily basis.
movies.title: Boyz n the Hood

movies.overview: A gangster, Nino, is in the Cash Money Brothers, making a million dollars every week selling crack. A cop, Scotty, discovers that the only way to infiltrate the gang is to become a dealer himself.
movies.title: New Jack City

movies.overview: A tribute to the controversial black activist and leader of the struggle for black liberation. He hit bottom during his imprisonment in the '50s, he became a Black Muslim and then a leader in the Nation of Islam. His assassination in 1965 left a legacy of self-determination and racial pride.
movies.title: Malcolm X

movies.overview: Marcus is a successful advertising executive who woos and beds women almost at will. After a company merger he finds that his new boss, the ravishing Jacqueline, is treating him in exactly the same way. Completely traumatised by this, his work goes badly downhill.
movies.title: Boomerang

movies.overview: Billy Hoyle and Sidney Deane are an unlikely pair of basketball hustlers. They team up to con their way across the courts of Los Angeles, playing a game that's fast dangerous - and funny.
movies.title: White Men Can't Jump

movies.overview: Four Harlem friends -- Bishop, Q, Steel and Raheem -- dabble in petty crime, but they decide to go big by knocking off a convenience store. Bishop, the magnetic leader of the group, has the gun. But Q has different aspirations. He wants to be a DJ and happens to have a gig the night of the robbery. Unfortunately for him, Bishop isn't willing to take no for answer in a game where everything's for keeps.
movies.title: Juice

movies.overview: The Candyman, a murderous soul with a hook for a hand, is accidentally summoned to reality by a skeptic grad student researching the monster's myth.
movies.title: Candyman
Poetic Justice
movies.overview: In this film, we see the world through the eyes of main character Justice, a young African-American poet. A mail carrier invites a few friends along for a long overnight delivery run.

movies.original_title: What's Love Got to Do with It
movies.title: What's Love Got to Do with It
movies.overview: A film about the singer Tina Turner and how she rose to stardom with her abusive husband Ike Turner and how she gained the courage to break free.
Sobering and incisive, this cautionary drama centers on a street tough 18-year-old facing a moral quandary while trying to turn his life around.
movies.title: Menace II Society

movies.overview: The story of a young man who must confront his own fears about love as well as his relationships with family and friends.
movies.title: Jason's Lyric

movies.overview: From Spike Lee comes this vibrant semi-autobiographical portrait of a school-teacher, her stubborn jazz-musician husband and their five kids living in '70s Brooklyn.
movies.title: Crooklyn
Bad Boys
movies.overview: Marcus Burnett is a hen-pecked family man. Mike Lowry is a foot-loose and fancy free ladies' man. Both are Miami policemen, and both have 72 hours to reclaim a consignment of drugs stolen from under their station's nose. To complicate matters, in order to get the assistance of the sole witness to a murder, they have to pretend to be each other.

When Blade's mother was bitten by a vampire during pregnancy, she did not know that she gave her son a special gift while dying—all the good vampire attributes in combination with the best human skills. Blade and his mentor battle an evil vampire rebel who plans to take over the outdated vampire council, capture Blade and resurrect a voracious blood god.
movies.title: Blade

movies.overview: Cheated on, mistreated and stepped on, the women are holding their breath, waiting for the elusive "good man" to break a string of less-than-stellar lovers. Friends and confidants Vannah, Bernie, Glo and Robin talk it all out, determined to find a better way to breathe.
movies.title: Waiting to Exhale

movies.overview: Craig and Smokey are two guys in Los Angeles hanging out on their porch on a Friday afternoon, smoking and drinking, looking for something to do.
movies.title: Friday

movies.overview: A strange funeral director tells four strange tales of horror with an African American focus to three drug dealers he traps in his place of business.
movies.title: Tales from the Hood

movies.overview: On the streets they call cash dead presidents. And that's just what a Vietnam veteran is after when he returns home from the war only to find himself drawn into a life of crime. With the aid of his fellow vets he plans the ultimate heist -- a daring robbery of an armored car filled with unmarked U.S. currency!
movies.title: Dead Presidents

movies.overview: Four black women, all of whom have suffered for lack of money and at the hands of the majority, undertake to rob banks. While initially successful, a policeman who was involved in shooting one of the women's brothers is on their trail. As the women add to the loot, their tastes and interests begin to change and their suspicions of each other increase on the way to a climactic robbery.
movies.title: Set It Off

movies.original_title: A Thin Line Between Love and Hate
movies.title: A Thin Line Between Love and Hate
movies.overview: Nightclub manager Darnell Wright is a perpetual playboy who is almost as devoted to his job as he is to the pursuit of beautiful women. After he sets his sights on the ultra-classy Brandi Web, he launches an all-out assault to win her heart. Ultimately, charm, lust and passion prevail, but Darnell learns the hard way that when you play, you pay. Brandi is much harder to get rid of than she was to get--especially when she realizes that she has a rival vying for Darnell's affection. When he finally decides to call it quits, Brandi becomes an obsessed femme fatale stalking the new love of her life.

movies.title: The Preacher's Wife
movies.overview: Good natured Reverend Henry Biggs finds that his marriage to choir mistress Julia is flagging, due to his constant absence caring for the deprived neighborhood they live in. On top of all this, his church is coming under threat from property developer Joe Hamilton. In desperation, Rev. Biggs prays to God for help - and help arrives in the form of an angel named Dudley.

movies.title: The Nutty Professor
movies.overview: Eddie Murphy stars as shy Dr. Sherman Klump, a kind, brilliant, 'calorifically challenged' genetic professor. When beautiful Carla Purty joins the university faculty, Sherman grows desperate to whittle his 400-pound frame down to size and win her heart. So, with one swig of his experimental fat-reducing serum, Sherman becomes 'Buddy Love', a fast-talking, pumped-up , plumped down Don Juan.

movies.title: Love Jones
movies.overview: Darius Lovehall is a young black poet in Chicago who starts dating Nina Moseley, a beautiful and talented photographer. While trying to figure out if they've got a "love thing" or are just "kicking it," they hang out with their friends, talking about love and sex. Then Nina tests the strength of Darius' feelings and sets a chain of romantic complications into motion.

movies.title: Booty Call
movies.overview: Rushon is sexually pent-up and ready to take thing things to the next level with his girlfriend, Nikki. But when he calls for a date, she asks to make it a double -- bringing along her brash friend Lysterine, whom Rushon sets up with his lewd buddy, Bunz. Things go better than expected. As the evening transitions from the restaurant to the bedroom, the two men go on a madcap search for what will surely make the night complete: condoms.

movies.title: Eve's Bayou
movies.overview: Summer heats up in rural Louisiana beside Eve’s Bayou, 1962, as the Batiste family tries to survive the secrets they’ve kept and the betrayals they’ve endured.

movies.title: Soul Food
movies.overview: Traditional Sunday dinners at Mama Joe's (Irma P. Hall) turn sour when sisters Teri (Vanessa L. Williams), Bird (Nia Long) and Maxine (Vivica A. Fox) start bringing their problems to the dinner table in this ensemble comedy. When tragedy strikes, it's up to grandson Ahmad (Brandon Hammond) to pull the family together and put the soul back into the family's weekly gatherings.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1990 to 2009
content_list.description: '90s independent cinema dominates the screens, and animation breaks new ground with Pixar. CGI reaches a new level with The Matrix, and Latin American and European cinemas capture the world's attention. Click here to see a chronological view of the main events in cinema from 1990 to 2009.
